projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Clarence Lindsco was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Clarence W. Lindsco. Clarence served in the U.S. Army's Fourth Division, 22nd Infantry Regiment, Company C. He served in the European theatre, and he is a veteran of D-Day. His highest rank was Private First Class. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at mr. Lindsco's home in Mentor, Ohio, on July 9, 2001. Clarence was 79 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your hometown during the war?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Fairport Harbor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And when did you -- when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I went into the service in July of 1941.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really. Drafted or did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I was a volunteer for one year, and then it turned into four and a half.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what did you volunteer for?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Anything. I was a kid. I didn't know which way up was at that time. I was 19 years old, so I volunteered for one year, and I didn't care where I went. And at the time people with no experience were going into the infantry. I couldn't be a pilot. I couldn't go in the Navy because I sailed on the lakes for one year, and I got sick as heck. So I couldn't -- I would have done that of course, you know, or the Merchant Marine. And 1941 I went to Columbus, Ohio, and from there I went to Fort Benning, Georgia. From there to Camp Gordon -- excuse me -- to Camp Wheeler, Georgia, near Augusta, and then to Camp Gordon. And then we went to a few places, Camp Gordon Johnston in Florida, to practice the invasion tactics. And eventually we found our way to Fort Dix for six great months, New York, Philadelphia, whatever, you know. And from there we went to a port of embarkation, Camp Kilmer -- I may have missed a few small ones but that's okay -- Camp Kilmer. And we got aboard the Capetown Castle, and we went to Liverpool, and it took us 14 days. And all the boiled eggs and wieners we could eat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get sick on that trip over?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No, sir. I don't get sick on the ocean. I get sick on the lakes, because the ocean goes like this and the lakes go like that. Anyway, we got to England and we went to a place called Exeter in England. And we were billeted in a soccer field stadium, and it had a little hut for changing clothes, and it had kwanset huts. And I lived in the little hut, and we trained there again. After that, we went to Southern England, Torquay, Portsmouth, and then across the water, the channel. The French call it the French Channel, the English call it the English Channel. And on D-Day, Fourth Division, which was my division, Company C, 22nd Infantry, First Battalion, First Platoon, First Squad, first scout. And as you know Utah Beach was comparatively mild compared to Omaha. Omaha had the 29th and the First Division, and they took a terrible beating. And our company went unscathed on D-Day, but then we went to the hedgerows. The hedgerows in France were barriers that divided farmers' fields. And some of them grew trees and roots, a perfect defense for the German Army. And we got through that and almost to Saint Lo, which was the breakout when everybody got going, Patton and his group, and our group, and all. Now, that's when I left the Fourth Division. I was wounded.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How were you wounded?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I was wounded in the leg, pelvis, and bladder, by a sniper. I don't want to talk too much about myself, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's what this is for. It's an oral history.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No. No. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's what makes your story unique.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: And this guy saved my life.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: That was just before Saint Lo and Santenay. And I was a scout ahead, and I got hit by a German sniper. And he saw that I couldn't move, and he come out and picked me up. And I was in a state of shock off and on. And I fought him because I thought he was German, but he was a 195-pound football player, so I lost. But anyway he took me to the aid station and he came right back. He didn't do that to get away from anything. And from the aid station I went to the hospital in England via boat across the channel. And while I was at -- well, they said we didn't have MASH units at the time, but we did. And that's where they performed the surgery, took the bullet out of my bladder, cut a hole in my stomach, and they said, "Okay. You go to the bathroom through that hole for a while." So I did, you know. And spent a number of months in England. And finally I walked in one day to the doctor's office, probably a major or a colonel, and he was pretending that he was hiding something, but he let me see that I was being transferred to the zone of the interior, which was the USA, and I was happy, you know. So I got out on the Queen Mary after, you know, being in the hospital for several months. And in four and a half days we were in New York Harbor. I went to Howard General Hospital, spent a while there, and then they tried to locate us as near to home as possible, so I went to Louisville, Kentucky. The hospital. What's the name of the hospital? Never mind. And from Louisville, I went to a discharge separation point, got my bird, and went home, and I'm here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Getting back to when you were wounded, when was that that you were wounded?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: July 9th. I only lasted 33 -- no -- 33 days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's a long time, though, for infantry.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah, I know, but some of them made it all the way through, Tom. And God bless them what they went through, because I am very interested in reading what happened from the time I left until the time they were finished. Our division had a turnover of 252 percent, 2.52 men for every original man. And this guy was very good. He came to visit me, Victor Corn.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Victor Corn.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: We have been corresponding, in touch since.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was he a buddy at all before this?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: He was in my -- not in my squad, in my platoon. So we weren't buddies, but we were together, you know. We were brought together. You know, during the war, we didn't fight as companies, we fought as smaller groups. And Victor Corn saved my life and allowed me to get married and have children. And after 47 years I got ahold of him and thanked him, and he came to visit me. And that got me up to 1990.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did he have any specific memories about the time he saved your life?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. It's all written in there. His memories were that he saw that I couldn't move. He knew that he could do something to help, and that's the way it was anyway. If you could help, you helped, you know. And he was a big man, a real big man. Carried me like a sack of potatoes back to the aid station, laid me under the tree. The doctor looked at me and he said, "Oh, it went on through." And I said, "Well, yeah, everything is okay." So I got to the -- I call it a MASH unit -- and we were sitting outside waiting to be tagged ordered, you know, severe, less severe, not severe. And I asked for a urinal and I filled it up with blood, so I got the severe. Went into the tent the same night, got -- I don't remember, Tom, whether there were candles, but they did that operation and removed that bullet. And what a wonderful thing they did. You know, I'm all for the US Army and its affiliates, like the VA Hospital, and what they did there. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job as first scout?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: First scout. When we got to a hedgerow, they were divided into squares, 100 x 200 yards. And when the scouts are out, get to the middle, and that's where you get terrified, Tom. I mean I was scared. And there was going over, you know, and pretty soon we moved on and -- well, I was scared all the time I was in France, you know. Now, like it says here, it says kind of to sum up, "The truth is 57 years have glossed it all over and given World War II a polish and a glow that it did not have at the time."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's one of the important things about doing this is I'm getting a very accurate picture of World War II, not Steven Spielberg's version. I like the movie, but, you know, it's not glory.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I saw the movie and -- I'm going to give you one gory detail.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: The first thing I saw as we were going in the causeway on Utah Beach was a paratrooper -- they went in at 12:00 in the morning -- hanging from a tree with his brain exposed. Now, I will never, never forget that. I saw a lot of other things, Tom, that is not going to be forgotten. My memory, you know. And I saw the dead cows, horses, German. I could sit on a German and eat my lunch really. And this happened sometime. And some of the guys -- I looked over and saw a young man leaning up against the tree, Gee, he's sleeping. No, he wasn't. He was dead. That was another division, the Ninth Division. And here is my diary.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You kept a diary?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yes, sir. In 1944 of our trip on the Queen Mary, four and one-half days. And it didn't need an escort because it was so fast that the submarines did not have time to take aim. Now, this lady wrote an article for The News Herald. She liked the Queen too, so I kept that. Tried to contact her but I never heard from her.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the feeling when you were approaching the beach there at Utah, when you were in the lining mount?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. I was so dumb I was helping another guy with his pack. I wasn't -- at that time -- and it took me about anywhere from three days to five to be afraid. The ones before that, the three to five, or the one to five, I wasn't. And I don't know why, but I guess I found out that they were -- they meant business. And I was so young, Tom, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you at that time?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I was 21.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any idea at the time of what was happening at Omaha?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: We knew nothing. We didn't know what was going on 50 feet on either side, Tom. And, you know, it's all history now, being dropped off on the beach and President -- or Roosevelt with his cane directing traffic. They said he didn't have a gun, but I read later that he had his .45. Roosevelt. Somebody said, "Yeah, do you remember him?" I said, "He was a big dummy."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you meet him?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No. I never met him. I have read about it, Tom. No. I never met him. You see, now, this is kind of important. The Eighth Infantry went in first on Utah Beach, 22nd went in second, the 12th went in third. So the Eighth took some casualties, being first, and we took less in the 12th, took less.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, when you -- when you -- again, I'm curious about how these hedgerows were taken. Did you have to have the specially-equiped tanks to get through them, or how were you able to --

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No. They couldn't do it. The tanks couldn't maneuver. And some bright young enlisted man said that, "Let's weld some prongs on the front of the tank." I'm shortening this up, we could be here --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, I have plenty of tape.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No. And they put those prongs on, they welded them on. And they were able to go right through those hedgerows with the tanks. If they went up like this, then they got hit in the underbelly and destroyed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other vivid memories of that month?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I have -- yeah, I have a few.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you want to share any of them? That's what we're here for.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Okay. Well, you know, World War II guys are starting to talk more because they're afraid we're going to be forgotten, and it's actually true. Now, when I was in Washington -- I'm going to throw this in --nobody talked about death or killing. We talked about where we were and this and, you know, what happened there and -- not who got killed, but just where we were. And I made it, he made it, and we all made it. No, we didn't all make it. And our ceremony in Washington was directed to the people that did not come home. They were the people that slept over there in France. And those are the people that we try to remember the most, you know. Because if it were me, you know, I would be sleeping in France, and I wouldn't have my daughters, and my children, my wife, my years. And those were the guys that were the -- don't call them heroes, they were just the guys, Tom.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: And I remember the first thing, I think the first time I got frightened, that I was between two hedgerows, and there was an officer near me. And they opened up, and the officer said, "I'm going to go get a tank." And, you know, they were flying, you know, I could hear them. Then he got the tank, and the tank opened up with .50 caliber machine gun, sprayed the whole hedgerows. We got up and walked back. And another time I was with the captain and he was standing behind a tree, and we had to take a certain hill. And I was on the ground. He was behind the tree, and the sniper was firing at him. Oh, man, ripped some clothes, canteen, but he couldn't get us because he wasn't at the right elevation. And the captain said to me, "Well, you better get him before he gets us." I didn't get him. I couldn't. And anyway we went on the hill. I didn't take the hill, the men took the hill, Tom, not me. And one other time I was in the middle, and I have a little twig that I was hiding behind, and I didn't lift up and fire, and I got kind of heck for that from my teammates. I couldn't. Too scared, you know. So there were a lot more, but even in one month there there were a lot of things that happened. And it's kind of glossed over, and you get -- well, things get dimmer and dimmer as years go by, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particular buddies or any things that you did with buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call and packages from home or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I used to get -- what did I like? I liked those nickel apple pies, and I got those from home in the States, not overseas. And, oh, usually some things were not perishable. And letters were awfully important, Tom, wherever you were. And when I was in the hospital, after I got hurt, my mother got this letter from someone that wrote it for me because I wasn't able. And you can't tell them, you know, that you're dying, you have to say everything is great.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you -- did you think it was pretty serious at the time? Did they tell you it was?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Oh, man, it was so serious.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A very serious wound, huh?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: See, if it goes through your bladder --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: But mine, the inertia from here to here, stopped it right in the middle of the bladder.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: And they took it out, removed it, and I had a long recovery. Bladder things had to heal up inside, outside, then I had a bowel obstruction as a result of the surgery, and that took a while. And then I had malaria, I think. Shouldn't have that on the eastern part of the continent. Either that or something else, and that was -- these were my hospital stays, you know. Part of the reason that I was there so long, you know. I had the bowel obstruction, I woke up -- or I didn't wake up one night. I started getting all this stuff up, because two weeks I says, "Nurse, give me a cup of coffee so I can go to the -- you're a procrastinator." I said, "No." She wouldn't. And I woke up about this far from, you know, and there goes another operation. I remember all the operations were done with an injection in the spine, spinal tap, whatever they call it, and I knew what was going on the second time. They took everything out, all my intestines. One of them said, "Hey, you must have had spaghetti yesterday." So they took them out, cut out whatever was necessary. I don't know whether it was two inches or two feet or what, and put them back together. And bladder, bowel, malaria, to simplify it that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you in England before D-Day?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: About six months.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you do over there for fun?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Practiced being a soldier. I was not involved, but our group went to Slapton Sands, and the Germans killed -- this was an exercise preparing for the landing on Utah Beach -- and the German subs killed 700 and some people. Now, that was kept a secret for years and years and years before they admitted that that happened. And that was from our group, but they were mostly engineers and maintenance men of that 700. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were the English people nice to you over there?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. I ate enough fish and chips and I drank stout and ale. And I went back a couple of years ago and drank some more stout and had some more fish and chips, and the English were nice, you know. You can read it in any book, the soldiers -- American soldiers are over here, overpaid and oversexed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: You know. And generally they were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You saw a lot of that with the outfit?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Guys having a little too much fun?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Uh-huh. I don't know if this can be off the record, but we alternated nights with the African Americans. They would go to town one night, and we -- another -- too much confusion, and that's the way it was. England was nice, it's a beautiful country. The only thing they care about in England is soccer, just like our baseball. And the people were generous to the extent of what they had, and they didn't have an awful lot. And they would be willing to do eggs for you, and play cards with you at night in their home, and invite you to their home on Sunday. And other than the racial discontent, the English people were very good to us. And I don't blame them a bit if they weren't good. I mean, you take that many people that come to your country, and it might be upsetting to have that happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have much contact with any French people when you were over in France?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: None. Oh, yeah. Maybe a French farmer here and a French farmer there. And I did drink a little bit of cognac, and always my excuse is that you can't drink the water. So, you know, I and many others, Tom, you know. And we -- in that 33 days, if you did meet a Frenchman, it was, like, on a black market basis. They wanted the shoes. And of cigarettes, we had a bunch, Tom, all we could use. We put cigarettes in our food, our sea rations, our K-Rations. Free. Some guy went on the Beach, Utah, with several cartons of cigarettes, but they were left on the beach. They were in his way, you know. So, oh, man.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were the few French people that you saw pretty thankful for the allies coming in?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Who? The French?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The French. The handful that you saw.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No. No, they weren't. The Fourth Division was the first division in Paris, and General de Gaulle took the credit for them; that was politics. And I guess I better not say that the French weren't good, I didn't have that much contact. I don't know. And in my readings, they had the French underground, and I think they did a lot, helped a lot, you know. And I'm reading a book now about President Roosevelt. Man, he was a rough guy, Tom. He wanted to be elected in 1940. He didn't want mobilization, he didn't want production, war production, and I'm still wondering if he knew that Pearl Harbor was going to happen. I have absolutely no reason to wonder, just in my reading, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, you were in the Army when Pearl Harbor was attacked, right?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yes, sir. I was in a little restaurant in Georgia having lunch. And I was getting ready to go home on my furlough. So I went back, I went to town to buy the tickets for the train to go home. I went back, the bunks were all rolled up. Ready, get ready. We were going. We were still there three years later. And I never missed a Christmas holiday at home in four and one-half years. Now, that's pretty hard for me to say that, but my furloughs came well and regularly. And they were probably ten days long, ten to 14. And I had overstayed one, Tom.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get in trouble?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Not much. Not much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your homecoming when you finally got out of the hospital and came back home?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: When I came home?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: There was no homecoming. You had a choice. You could take 52 weeks, 20 bucks a week. I went to work in three weeks. And I tried to resume my normal life. There was some things that were -- well, I was glad to be home, so they weren't hard, but they were difficult. For example, I was in the shop, they had a way of punching holes in steel and sounded just like a gun, and that upset me for a while. And I had my children. My wife pass away eight years ago. I have two daughters within five miles of me, and they watch over me too close. Had me moved. That has nothing to do with, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. So did you have to deal with any of the dreams and things like that when you came back?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No, sir. Never.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were fortunate with that.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Not one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just other kinds of reminders?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I went -- had one bad experience. Do you know about _____________Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Pearl Harbor Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I guess I do know that.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I went there a while back and something triggered me. And I don't know what it was, Tom, but anyway, it got me down for a couple of days. I want to put a plug in for the VA Hospital. Can I?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. I've got good feelings for them too with what they did with my dad.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Okay. Three years ago this month I was diagnosed with cancer of the esophagus and the stomach this way, you know. I go over here, oh, in the radiation and chemotherapy, and I thought about that for a while. I'm too vain to lose my hair, so I said -- the VA said that they would do it without all that monkey business. And three years later I'm here. It was a ten-hour thing, you know. And I still go back for checkups, and I take 13 pills a day, but I'm thankful for the VA. And another thing when I got out of the service, I was chosen -- not chosen, but under Public Law 16 I went into a draftsman apprenticeship for four years. This is service connected. And they paid me a certain amount, up to what -- part of what I might make after I finished. And by golly, I stayed with the same company. Including service time, I had 42 years. Diamond, now __________ Diamond Shamrock and Access Energy, and they treated me good too. I'm a fortunate person, Tom.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes, you are.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I am really. And I'm -- it's good to be home. Now we're going to shut this off. We're through.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories that come to mind before we shut it off?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I don't go into gory things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't? You don't really care to?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I don't. No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They're still there though?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they're there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You just don't care to share them?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Some guys do, some guys don't.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: I don't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I have got a couple of guys that they seem to have no problem with just telling me all this stuff. And then just the other night, I had a guy that he wanted me to shut the tape off. He wanted to tell me the memory, but he didn't want it on the tape.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Off the record. Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And it wasn't anything that had to be off the record, I think he didn't want that memory -- he wanted to control when the memory came up.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: If it's on tape then it's there.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: It's there. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So I think that was part of what he was trying to say. But I have heard some amazing, very, very incredible real pictures of war since I have started doing this.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because I think I have talked to almost 30 veterans now.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Have you?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. And I know the guy that was in the Engineers Battalion at Omaha.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Omaha.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Talked to him the other day. Guys who have been through the Battle of Bulge, so --

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Well, my outfit went through all of those, _________ Forest, Bulge, they were first on the Siegfried line, first in Paris. And our good president stopped us and said, "Well, let the Russians go in." And this is all from reading now. And that's where we stopped and they went in. And the big wall went up, big wall came down. And I went to Germany too recent -- not recently, 1973.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember having any reaction when you heard the news that FDR had died?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Everybody had a reaction. I didn't cry. It wasn't that significant to me. Some people cried, some people cheered, you know. And it was just something that happened to our leader, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that's something that I think has been distorted in what I know about history, because what you're telling me is what the vast majority of the guys tell me.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Sure. I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: History has it that everybody just broke down, that it was so terrible that the world stopped and everyone cried, and that's not what I'm hearing.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And there have been a few that have been still rather angry at him because of the Pearl Harbor thing.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I mean there's still some people --

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: This book that I'm reading will tell you in detail about how he opposed and we could have mobilized so many years earlier and been ready. And he did a lot of things to be elected. And he put people in a position that were opposites, not together, for a reason, so that things would go his way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Divide and conquer.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. That's what he did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So he was a smart political man.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. He was smart.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's for sure.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: For 12 years you have to be smart.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not necessarily the great valiant leader that history would paint him to be.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Well, let people decide that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. People decide.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. I think they need to listen to this and also try to put it a little bit more in perspective.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. Let them decide.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever meet Eisenhower or anything? END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Eisenhower. I had no true contact with the man, but, you know, we would stand and he would walk by and eyes right and salute. And Bradley, and even -- what's his name? Monty.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Monty?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Monty Montgomery. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the opinion of American GIs on Monty?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: He was too cautious. Maybe that was all right, maybe he saved some of his men by being cautious, but he lost a lot of time getting into Caen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: An awful lot. He was supposed to be there on D-Day. Took him, I don't know, weeks to get there. And that's my impression of him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's the impression --

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Of Eisenhower, he was a master at pulling people together. That was his biggest trait. I don't think he was a great general, he was just a great person to be able to get people to agree and work together and, hey, we needed that, didn't we? Sure. Bradley was the soldier's soldier. He was the first Army. And I had no personal contact with him, but I know from my reading that he was a good -- one of the best generals that we had, the soldier's soldier. By that I mean, he was for the soldiers, you know. And the infantry had a tough job, Tom, but heck, now the question is at that time you couldn't do anything without the infantry. Couldn't do anything without the infantry at Vietnam or Korea. Now -- or the Gulf a little bit. Now I wonder if we're going to need anybody. Our good president is trying to shoot down the missiles, and he's doing a good job.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think of Patton?

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Patton? I think he was a SOB. I wasn't in the tent, but that should never have happened. I was in a hospital ward where they still -- where the legs were off, still used maggots to eat that dead flesh. And the war brought us penicillin, some antibiotics. And I don't know, Tom, they say it was the great war. Civil War was a great war, so was the Revolutionary War, so was Vietnam, so was Korea, so was the Persian Gulf. As long as there are men that are injured and killed, this is war. You know what, Tom, I can't understand how Adolf Hitler had people, that many following him, that he was able to do what he was able to do. And I don't understand why people want war. And the only reason people want war I guess is because if somebody has something that you want, I liken that to a barstool. If you go into a bar and sit on a stool, somebody comes along and says, "Hey, that's my stool," and then a big fight. That's war, like war. And I can't understand at all how he had that many people following him. You know, I read The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich. I read it a lot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But World War II was very unique. It was the last war of the century where it was really a battle of good versus evil.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Yeah. I know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There are shades of good and evil on each side.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: Oh, my, yes. And Hitler made two mistakes. The first mistake was he waited too long to go into Russia and his troops got cold. And the other mistake is that he let Gordon talk him into believing that they could take England by air. And, Tom, if that hadn't have happened and they got to England, I just wonder what the world would be, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: He made those two grave errors. He made other mistakes, but those two were the greatest yet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: If he had taken England there would be no place, no base of operation.

sp.speaker: Clarence Lindsco
sp.p: No place to hide.
